newsitem.title: USA: Reebok shareholders vote for cutting directors' terms.
newsitem.headline: Reebok shareholders vote for cutting directors' terms.

text.p: Shareholders of Reebok International Ltd., stung by falling market share in recent years, voted on Thursday against management and for a proposal to cut directors' terms to make them more accountable.
Fifty-three percent of shareholders who voted approved the proposal, put forward by the nation's largest public pension fund, to cut directors' terms to one year from the current three years.

The California Public Employees' Retirement System (Calpers), which owns about 599,000 shares of Reebok, warned in February it would target the footwear manufacturer and that the board of directors could face a fight for reelection if they did not improve performance.
Reebok Chief Executive Paul Fireman said following the meeting that the board of directors would take the vote under consideration, but he remains opposed to the measure.
"It's certainly not an overwhelming majority, but we will take it into consideration," Fireman said.

The vote was a victory for institutional shareholders, some of whom had voiced their displeasure with Reebok management at recent shareholder meetings or had grown frustrated with the company and sold their shares.

Peter Russ, an analyst from Shelby, Collum, Davis & Co. who represents some institutional customers, said the shareholder vote should serve as a warning to Stoughton, Mass.-based Reebok, the nation's second-largest athletic footwear manufacturer.
"Thank God for Calpers," he said. "That's very unusual. That's a real sign of shareholder unrest."
Fireman, who told disgruntled shareholders last year that he would turn the company around in two years or step aside, said in his speech Thursday that the company is showing signs of improvement.

Athletic footwear sales are strengthening, inventories are in good shape and apparel and leisure shoe sales are growing, said Fireman, who along with his wife owns about 21 percent of the outstanding shares and options.

"I do believe we are a much different company than we were a year ago," Fireman said. "We are clearly heading in the right direction, we have a lot of work to do. By no means have we accomplished all the results."
Despite his reassuring words, several shareholders voiced their displeasure.
Calpers, which manages $110 billion in assets, said in February that Reebok has been in a "financial free fall" and that management has operated with "insufficient accountability" to the board.

Its proposal, if adopted by Reebok, would eliminate a "staggered" or "classified" board, whereby directors serve three-year terms and one-third of the board is up for election at a given time. In its place would be a "declassified" board with one-year terms.
Calpers said in its supporting statement in the Reebok proxy form that a classified board "insulates its members from immediate challenge" and hampers accountability.
A Calpers spokesman said the pension fund would first confirm the figures before commenting.

Fireman said a board with one-year terms might be in the interests of institutional shareholders when there is a takeover of a company and the directors can be quickly voted out of office all at once.
But he said there is no "takeover talk" of Reebok.

"I think the staggered board (with three-year terms) is much, much in the best interests of the shareholders," Fireman said. "I think it will realise for them the best value in any way we go forward."
Reebok's stock rose 12.5 cents to $38.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
